courses.title: Your first client content pack
courses.summary: A written walkthrough for turning one approved recording into a small, reviewed content package. Finish with a sample deliverable and a clear offer you can discuss with a real client.
outcomes: Define a small deliverable a client can evaluate
Create a draft from an approved source without inventing facts
Use a human review checklist before delivery
Package the work into a clear service offer

lessons.title: Pick one client problem
lessons.body: Start with a person who already has something worth saying: a consultant, creator, local business owner, or instructor. Ask which approved recording they want to reuse and who should see the finished content. Define a small package: one short summary, three social post drafts, and one email draft. Get permission to use the recording and agree on what information must stay private. Your first visible result is a written brief—not a promised sale. Write down the audience, the source, the tone, the deliverables, and the review deadline. If you do not have a client yet, practice on your own recording and label the result a sample.

lessons.title: Create a draft with a clear source
lessons.body: Transcribe the approved recording using a tool you already have access to. Read the transcript and correct names, dates, and any obvious transcription errors. Then ask your AI tool: ‘Using only this approved transcript, draft a 100-word summary, three distinct social posts, and one short email. Keep the speaker’s meaning. Do not invent claims, results, quotes, prices, or links. Mark uncertain details as NEEDS REVIEW. For each draft, identify the source passage that supports it.’ Keep the transcript, the prompt, and the drafts together. This is the first useful artifact: a traceable draft pack you can inspect.

lessons.title: Make the human review count
lessons.body: Compare every claim against the source. Check names, numbers, links, spelling, permissions, and tone. Remove repeated ideas and any claim the source does not support. Read the drafts aloud; they should sound like the client, not a generic advertisement. Keep a short change log so the client can see what you corrected. If an agent is helping, leave sending and publishing disabled until a person approves the final version. Share the draft pack for review through the client’s agreed process. A draft is not an approval, and an approval is not a payment receipt.

lessons.title: Turn the result into a clear offer
lessons.body: Describe exactly what the client receives, the source length you will accept, the turnaround you can meet, and the number of revisions included. Agree on the fee and payment terms before paid work begins. Track preparation time and any tool costs so the service makes sense for you. After delivery, ask whether the package saved the client time and what should change next time. A completed sample can help start that conversation; it does not guarantee an order. When you are ready to manage repeated jobs, use SSS Brain as the place to monitor the workflow and human approvals. Solo starters can use Brainiak templates to organize the first version. Cut the noise, and let's put it on the board.
